overview: This record represents Spain’s northern protectorate in Morocco, created by the Franco-Spanish agreement of November 1912 and ended in 1956. The map shows only 1914 to 1920, a short slice of that history. Its northern outline should not be confused with Spanish Sahara or the separate southern protectorate zone. Formal colonial boundaries also concealed areas where Moroccan resistance prevented effective Spanish control.

periods.title: A contested protectorate
periods.summary: The 1912 agreement established the protectorate, but its boundaries were not a record of completed conquest.

periods.title: War in the Rif
periods.summary: The Spanish defeat at Annual in 1921 was followed by Franco-Spanish campaigns; the war continued until 1927.

periods.title: Colonial administration and growing institutions
periods.summary: Schools, workshops and services developed within an unequal colonial administration.

periods.title: Moroccan independence
periods.summary: The declaration of 7 April 1956 recognized Morocco’s independence and provided for transferring authority.

sections.title: Government, resistance and a written sample

items.text: The protectorate kept Moroccan authorities while placing them under Spanish supervision. The 1916 regulations empowered the high commissioner to authorize or suspend the khalifa’s decrees and control his government’s official foreign contacts. The legal machinery makes the imbalance of power clearer than the reassuring word “protectorate.”

The official gazette of 6 December 1912 prints “Convenio entre España y Francia,” meaning “Agreement between Spain and France.” The phrase occurs in a decree seeking parliamentary authorization to ratify the agreement of 27 November. It is an attested Spanish administrative sample from the creation of the protectorate.

Spain’s defeat at Annual in 1921 exposed the gap between a claimed protectorate and control on the ground. The later Alhucemas landing in 1925 formed part of a joint Franco-Spanish offensive. Fighting continued until 1927, so the map’s disappearance of this label in 1920 is especially misleading.

During the Rif War, Abdelkrim sought recognition for a local Red Cross or Red Crescent and appealed for outside medical assistance. French and Spanish resistance obstructed these projects. A planned international mission was overtaken by his surrender in 1926: caring for civilians was entangled with arguments about who had the right to govern.

Early Spanish schools did not always have trained teachers or a settled curriculum. Soldiers, officials and consular staff sometimes taught, and facilities could be poor. A teaching board created in 1913 tried to organize this uneven system. Opening a classroom and providing a dependable education were two different achievements.

Inspectors in 1914 recommended paying Spanish-language teachers in the Alliance Israélite schools of Tetouan and Larache. Their report also proposed improving Muslim teacher training and secondary education; many recommendations waited years. The document reveals distinct Jewish and Muslim educational institutions, alongside Spanish ambitions to shape what children learned.

Tetouan’s Dar Sanaa craft school opened in 1919. Antonio Got’s plan proposed free instruction and materials, entry from age twelve, and places reserved mainly for local pupils. Its workshops covered wood, leather, metal, cloth and ceramics. Learning could mean making a useful object rather than filling another page of exercises.

The same workshop plan respected Muslim prayer times and anticipated Muslim, Jewish and Christian pupils sharing the school. It recognized that agreeing on a weekly rest day would be tricky. Masters were to keep records of each apprentice’s materials and working time, turning skilled handwork into a carefully documented education.

sections.title: Health, everyday movement and continuing craft

items.text: Clinic reports from Nador and Zoco El Had describe vaccination campaigns that included schoolchildren. The Nador report recorded 998 vaccinations in 1913. These records give a concrete glimpse of attempts to prevent smallpox, while remaining reports by colonial doctors rather than a count of every child protected across the Rif.

The same doctors treated wounds, fractures and other surgical problems using local anesthesia. Patients needing major operations were sent to the hospital at Melilla. They also performed dental work. A small clinic therefore depended on a wider network: some problems could be handled locally, while others required a difficult journey.

The protectorate’s public-health organization assigned officials such tasks as checking drinking water, studying underground sanitation and considering healthier housing. These were formal responsibilities, not proof that every household received clean water. They show how staying well depended on streets, buildings and water supplies as well as doctors.

The independence agreement of April 1956 also changed ordinary travel: its additional protocol abolished visas and administrative formalities for moving between Morocco’s zones. Political reunification could therefore affect a family journey or a trader’s trip, as well as the names on government offices.

Dar Sanaa outlived the protectorate. Morocco’s culture ministry describes its continuing work training students from Tetouan and nearby places in threatened traditional crafts, alongside a museum of handmade objects. Skills passed from teacher to learner are a living part of the region’s heritage, not simply souvenirs of colonial rule.

ending.text: Spain recognized Moroccan independence on 7 April 1956 and agreed to transfer its authorities’ powers to the Moroccan government. This ended the northern protectorate. Communities, workshops and schools continued within independent Morocco; the imported 1920 endpoint marks neither independence nor disappearance.
